title: Storybook Parts
objectives: I can find the title and a page in a book.
I can tell about a character in a story.
I can tell a problem and a surprise in a story.
rationale: These are the words children need to talk about any picture book. Title and page name the parts of a book children can point to; character, problem, and surprise name the people and the turns that make a story work. All five have other everyday meanings, so the unit teaches the book sense of each and says so plainly. The unit revisits excited, nervous, grow, and sprout, since characters have feelings and stories can grow from a small beginning.

passage.title: Ana and The Lost Kite
paras: Ana opens a new book. The title is The Lost Kite.
A small fox is the main character. On the first page, he has a problem. His kite is stuck in a tree.
Ana turns the page, and a bird flies down with a surprise.

teacher.overview: Children learn five book words by holding picture books, then hear them in a short story about a fox and a kite and say them in short sentences. The unit is spoken and visual; no reading is needed.

notes.va.title.n: Hold up a book cover and say 'This is the title, the name of the book'. Title has other meanings, such as a title for a person, which are not taught here. Ask children to make up a title for a picture.
notes.va.page.n: Show that a page is one side of a sheet. Children may call the whole book a page. Count the pages with them and turn them one at a time. Page can also mean to call someone on a speaker, which is not taught.
notes.va.character.n: Character can mean a letter or a person's good traits, which are not taught here. Use animals and people in a favorite read-aloud. Ask 'Who is in the story?' before using the word.
notes.va.problem.n: Use a book with a clear problem, such as a lost object. Problem here is something to fix; do not use it for math problems yet. Say 'What is the problem? How do they fix it?' together.
notes.va.surprise.n: Use a wrapped box to show a surprise. Surprise is a noun here, something unexpected. Children may mix it up with excited; say a surprise can make you excited or nervous.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: 'This is the title of the book, the name on the cover. I turn the page. Here is a fox. The fox is a character. He has a problem. His kite is stuck! What will happen? A bird comes. That is a surprise!'
discuss: What problem does your favorite character have?
How can a surprise make a character feel nervous or excited?
misconceptions: The title is on every page.
A character is only a person.
A problem in a story is always sad.
extend: Make a class story map with a title, characters, a problem, and a surprise.
Have children draw their own page for a story and say the problem aloud.
teacher.reviewAdvice: Revisit excited and nervous by asking how characters feel when the problem and the surprise come. Revisit grow and sprout with a story about a seed that grows into a plant. Use problem and surprise again in unit 12 for fairy tales.

wida.oral: Partner A holds a picture book closed and says, 'I see a title.' Partner B names the title, then they open to a page and name a character and a problem.

needsReview: Spanish glosses (título, página, personaje, problema, sorpresa) have not been reviewed by a native speaker; título and página are cognates, but personaje is not the same as character in some uses.

Sense boundary: title (name of a book), page (one side of a sheet), character (a person or animal in a story), and surprise (something unexpected) are taught in their book senses only; other meanings are named in the teacher notes and left out.
Sense boundary: problem is taught as something to fix in a story, not as a math problem.
